claim: For the 2023-24 cycle, selective colleges responded to SFFA by adding identity/diversity/adversity supplemental prompts: among the top ~65 colleges studied by Sonja Starr, 43 had such prompts (up from 35), mandatory questions on those topics rose from 21 to 31, and identity-specific mandatory questions rose from 11 to 17. Most new prompts use indirect, open-ended framing ('lived experience,' 'adversity,' 'community,' 'perspective') rather than asking about race directly. The Common App's own personal-statement prompts were NOT changed.

application.content: Read a 'lived experience / community / perspective' supplement as an invitation, not a demand for a race-or-trauma confession. Decision rule: answer it with whatever community or formative experience genuinely shaped the student's character and what they'd add to campus — that can be racial/cultural identity, but it can equally be a neighborhood, a disability, a family role, a faith, or an intellectual community. The prompt rewards specificity and contribution-orientation, not category-disclosure.

Map the supplement back to the SFFA hinge before drafting: identify (a) the specific community/experience, (b) the quality or value it built, (c) how that quality will show up in this college's community. Answering all three is what converts an 'amorphous' diversity prompt into a passage an AO can legitimately credit — and it works whether or not race is the subject.

sources.citation: Sonja Starr, 'Admissions Essays After SFFA' (Indiana Law Journal vol. 100, iss. 3) — counts of 43 vs 35 colleges, 31 vs 21 mandatory, 17 vs 11 identity-specific; reported in Inside Higher Ed

connections.note: The new prompts are the institutional surface where the carve-out is exercised.
Overlaps the 'why-us / community / perspective' supplement craft: the post-SFFA carve-out is exercised through the Why-Us supplement, whose dominant failure mode this entry documents.

Specific named-school prompt texts independently verified by fetching the Inside Higher Ed 2023-08-02 article, which quotes Columbia, Babson, UMass Amherst, Brandeis, and Emory prompts verbatim.
